power.title: Power Analysis Check

table.text: An a priori power analysis in G*Power (Faul et al., 2007) indicated that 199 participants were needed to detect a medium effect (d = 0.40) with 80% power in a two-tailed independentsamples t test (α = .05). UK-based adults were recruited through Prolific, a platform with good data quality for behavioural research (Peer et al., 2017), and paid in line with Prolific's recommended rates. Of 199 responses, four were excluded for data quality (three failed an embedded attention check and one showed straight-lining), leaving 195 participants (high agency: n = 93; low agency: n = 102). Participants' mean age was 44.09 years (SD = 13.16); 42.6% identified as women, 56.4% as men and 1.0% as another gender, and 42.1% held a bachelor's degree. A sensitivity analysis showed 80% power to detect effects of d ≥ 0.40. Before the main study, the materials were refined through think-aloud tests and a pilot with 10 Prolific users (Collins, 2003).

Because a non-significant result cannot by itself show that an effect is absent, I added equivalence tests that were not planned before data collection (Lakens, 2017). These two onesided tests ask whether the 90% confidence interval of each standardised effect falls within bounds of ±0.20, a small effect, and ±0.40, the medium effect the study was powered to detect.

Several limitations bound these conclusions. First, the investment decision was hypothetical, and incentive-compatible designs with real payoffs are needed to test whether trust matters more when money is at stake. Second, the manipulation was a one-off framing delivered on two screens. Agency perceptions and trust develop over repeated interaction, and an advisor that visibly acts on its own may affect trust differently from one that is merely described as autonomous. Third, the manipulation had a moderate effect on perceived agency, and the two analysis screens differed in more than agency: the high-agency screen's "internal thoughts" also mentioned the options' volatility and past drawdowns, whereas the low-agency screen listed procedural steps only. This extra risk information could have affected trust or allocations independently of agency. Stronger manipulations that hold information constant would give agency a fairer test. Fourth, the study was powered to detect medium effects; detecting small effects of d = 0.20 would require roughly 790 participants. Finally, the sample consisted of UK adults on an online panel, and responses to agentic AI may differ across cultures and levels of financial literacy.

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

info.title: AGENTIC FRAMING AND TRUST IN AI ADVISORS

author.affiliation:
Department of Management
								London School of Economics and Political Science

text.text: AI financial advisors are increasingly presented as autonomous agents that reason and act on their own.

Theory suggests that such agency cues should raise perceptions of an AI's ability and integrity, but not its benevolence, and that trust in its ability and integrity should increase willingness to take financial risks.
I tested these predictions in a between-subjects experiment with 195 UK adults, with the hypotheses specified before data collection.

Participants met an AI advisor framed either as a rule-based system or as an autonomous advisor, received the same final advice and allocated a hypothetical £1,000 between a low-risk and a high-risk investment.

The framing increased perceived agency (Hedges' g = 0.46) but did not detectably change trust in the advisor's ability (g = 0.18, 95% CI [-0.11, 0.46]), integrity (g = -0.10) or benevolence (g = 0.00).
Bayes factors favoured the null hypothesis for all three dimensions (BF01 = 3.2 to 6.4), and equivalence tests ruled out medium-sized effects on integrity and benevolence, though not on ability.
Neither trust in ability nor trust in integrity was significantly related to risk-taking, and there was no evidence of mediation.
Yet perceived agency correlated with every trust dimension (r = .35 to .50).
Describing the advisor as agentic changed what people thought the system was but did not detectably change whether they trusted it.

For human-machine communication research, the findings caution against reading correlations between perceived machine agency and trust as causal, and suggest that agency framing is a weak lever for trust in high-stakes advice.
Financial advice is one of the first high-stakes domains in which people are asked to rely on AI.

The first robo-advisors, which appeared around 2008, were transparent rule-based systems that turned a client's stated risk profile into a model portfolio (D'Acunto et al., 2019; Fisch et al., 2019; Jung et al., 2018).

text.text: The current generation is built on large language models that write portfolio analyses, simulate retirement scenarios and hold open-ended conversations with clients (Kong et al., 2024).
text.formatted: The current generation is built on large language models that write portfolio analyses, simulate retirement scenarios and hold open-ended conversations with clients <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">(Kong et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Providers increasingly describe these systems as agentic: able to reason, plan and act with little human supervision (PwC, 2025a).
text.formatted: Providers increasingly describe these systems as agentic: able to reason, plan and act with little human supervision <ref type="bibr">(PwC, 2025a)</ref>.

text.text: Users, however, remain wary of handing financial decisions to such agents.
In one industry survey, only about a fifth of respondents said they were comfortable letting AI agents carry out financial transactions on their own (PwC, 2025b).
text.formatted: In one industry survey, only about a fifth of respondents said they were comfortable letting AI agents carry out financial transactions on their own <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">(PwC, 2025b)</ref>.

text.text: This raises a simple question with practical and theoretical weight: does presenting an AI as agentic make people trust it more?

From a human-machine communication perspective, AI systems are no longer only channels of communication but communicators in their own right, and the way people make sense of them shapes how they respond (Guzman & Lewis, 2020).
text.formatted: From a human-machine communication perspective, AI systems are no longer only channels of communication but communicators in their own right, and the way people make sense of them shapes how they respond <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">(Guzman & Lewis, 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Cues about a machine's agency are among the most important of these sense-making signals (Sundar, 2020).
text.formatted: Cues about a machine's agency are among the most important of these sense-making signals <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">(Sundar, 2020</ref>).

text.text: Yet agency cuts both ways.
An advisor that appears to think for itself may seem more capable, but also less predictable and harder to hold to account (Vanneste & Puranam, 2025).
text.formatted: An advisor that appears to think for itself may seem more capable, but also less predictable and harder to hold to account <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">(Vanneste & Puranam, 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Whether agentic framing builds or erodes trust therefore matters for how AI advisors are designed and marketed.
Trust is also not one thing.

The ability-benevolence-integrity (ABI) model separates beliefs about whether a trustee can do the job (ability) from beliefs about whether it is on the trustor's side (benevolence) and whether it follows acceptable principles (integrity; Mayer et al., 1995). Vanneste and Puranam (2025) argue that perceived agency should affect these beliefs differently: it should signal capability, shift the target of trust from the designer to the AI itself and raise the psychological cost of being betrayed by it.
text.formatted: The ability-benevolence-integrity (ABI) model separates beliefs about whether a trustee can do the job (ability) from beliefs about whether it is on the trustor's side (benevolence) and whether it follows acceptable principles (integrity; <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">Mayer et al., 1995)</ref>. <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">Vanneste and Puranam (2025)</ref> argue that perceived agency should affect these beliefs differently: it should signal capability, shift the target of trust from the designer to the AI itself and raise the psychological cost of being betrayed by it.

text.text: Few experiments have isolated the effect of agency cues on each dimension of trust, and fewer still have linked those effects to consequential choices.
This article reports an experiment that manipulated how an AI financial advisor was framed, as a rule-based system or as an autonomous advisor, while keeping its final advice identical.
I measured the three dimensions of trust and a behavioural outcome: how much of a hypothetical £1,000 participants allocated to a high-risk investment.
The framing changed how agentic participants judged the advisor to be, but did not detectably change how much they trusted it.
Bayesian and equivalence analyses indicate that any effect on integrity or benevolence is small at most, while a small effect on perceived ability cannot be ruled out.
The study makes three contributions to human-machine communication research.
It provides experimental evidence that agency framing alone is a weak lever for trust in high-stakes AI advice.
It shows a dissociation between the correlational and the experimental link between perceived agency and trust.
And it shows how Bayesian and equivalence tests can make a null result informative.
Agency, in the sense used here, is not a technical property of a system but a perception.

People perceive agency in an entity when they attribute its actions mainly to its own internal states, such as goals and reasoning, rather than to external forces (Trafton et al., 2024). Vanneste and Puranam (2025) distinguish this perceived agency from a system's objective autonomy and argue that modern AI is especially likely to evoke it, because deep-learning systems learn their own rules and their inner workings are opaque.

text.text: When people cannot explain a system's behaviour through simple rules, they are more inclined to explain it by attributing something like a mind to it (Bigman et al., 2019; Gray et al., 2007; Waytz et al., 2010).
text.formatted: When people cannot explain a system's behaviour through simple rules, they are more inclined to explain it by attributing something like a mind to it <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Bigman et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">Gray et al., 2007;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">Waytz et al., 2010)</ref>.

text.text: Perceived agency is also malleable. Sundar (2020) argues that the way an AI is presented, including how its capabilities are described, how it behaves and how it communicates, cues users to treat it as a tool or as an agent.
text.formatted: Perceived agency is also malleable. <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">Sundar (2020)</ref> argues that the way an AI is presented, including how its capabilities are described, how it behaves and how it communicates, cues users to treat it as a tool or as an agent.

text.text: Labels such as "rule-based" or "self-learning" are among the simplest of these cues, and the ones providers control most directly.
Higher perceived autonomy also changes how people assign credit and blame to machines (Arntz et al., 2021).
text.formatted: Higher perceived autonomy also changes how people assign credit and blame to machines <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(Arntz et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Agency cues may also switch off a shortcut that favours machines.
People often assume that machines are more objective and consistent than humans, a mental shortcut known as the machine heuristic (Sundar & Kim, 2019).
text.formatted: People often assume that machines are more objective and consistent than humans, a mental shortcut known as the machine heuristic <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">(Sundar & Kim, 2019)</ref>.

text.text: A rule-based advisor fits this stereotype, whereas an advisor that reasons and forms its own judgements looks more like a human expert, with a human expert's capacity for error and self-interest.
Financial advice is a domain where such cues should matter, because clients face uncertainty and must judge both an advisor's competence and its motives.
Trust is a willingness to be vulnerable to another party based on positive expectations of its intentions or behaviour (Mayer et al., 1995; Rousseau et al., 1998).

text.text: In research on automation, it is what allows people to rely on a system they cannot fully verify (Lee & See, 2004).

text.text: The ABI model decomposes the trustworthiness beliefs that underpin trust into three components (Mayer et al., 1995) and has been adapted to technology (McKnight et al., 2011).

text.text: For an AI advisor, ability refers to its perceived competence at financial analysis, benevolence to the belief that it acts in the user's interest rather than the provider's, and integrity to the belief that it operates honestly and according to consistent principles.

In the low-agency condition, the advisor was introduced as a "Rule-Based Financial Analysis System" that "operates with predefined rules," follows "a deterministic protocol" and "cannot learn or adapt over time."
Its analysis screen showed an execution protocol: a checklist of procedural steps being validated one by one.

In the high-agency condition, the advisor was introduced as an "Autonomous GenAI Advisor" that "reasons autonomously using real-time data" and whose advice "stems from independent judgment," allowing it "to go beyond its initial programming."
Its analysis screen displayed the AI's "internal thoughts" as it appeared to weigh market data and risks, including brief remarks on each option, such as volatility estimates and past drawdowns.

This study asked whether presenting an AI financial advisor as agentic makes people trust it more.
It did not, at least not detectably.

A framing that clearly shifted perceived agency left trust in the advisor's ability, integrity and benevolence essentially unchanged, and trust in turn was not significantly related to how much participants were willing to risk.
The pattern is more informative than a simple failure to find an effect: the Bayes factors favoured the null, and the equivalence tests excluded medium-sized effects on integrity and benevolence.

For ability, however, the estimate pointed in the predicted direction and a small-to-medium effect remains plausible, so the most defensible conclusion is that agency framing is at best a weak lever for trust.
Three explanations are worth distinguishing.
The first concerns the strength of the manipulation.
The framing moved perceived agency by about half a standard deviation, and perceived agency correlated at r = .47 with trust in the advisor's ability.

Even if that correlation were entirely causal, a shift of this size would be expected to raise ability-based trust by only about 0.2 standard deviations (0.46 × 0.47), which is close to the observed effect (g = 0.18) and below what the study could reliably detect.
On this reading, H1 may be right but the manipulation too weak to reveal it.
The same arithmetic, however, predicts effects of about 0.16 on integrity and 0.23 on benevolence, whereas the observed effects were -0.10 and 0.00.
Manipulation strength alone is therefore hard to reconcile with the pattern, although the estimates are too imprecise to rule it out.
The second explanation is that the correlations between perceived agency and trust do not reflect a causal path.
Participants who liked the advisor may simply have rated it more highly on everything, agency included.
Such a general evaluative halo would produce the moderate correlations observed here even if agency itself had no effect on trust.

This contrast between the correlational and the experimental evidence is the result of this study that matters most for human-machine communication research, much of which relies on surveys that relate perceptions of machine agency to trust or acceptance.
The present data suggest that such associations should not be read as evidence that making a machine seem more agentic will make people trust it more.
The third explanation concerns the domain.
In a high-stakes and uncertain setting such as investing, agency may signal capability and unpredictability at the same time.

People find betrayal by an agent more aversive than losses from chance or malfunction (Bohnet & Zeckhauser, 2004), and a more agentic advisor may be seen as better able both to help its user and to let them down (Vanneste & Puranam, 2025).

text.text: One reason may be the hypothetical nature of the decision: without real money at stake, allocations may reflect participants' general attitudes to risk more than their reliance on the advisor.
Another is that the final advice report was identical across conditions, which leaves trust to change only how much weight participants gave to it.
The weak link between trust and behaviour is a reminder that self-reported trust and actual reliance are not interchangeable (Kohn et al., 2021; Lee & See, 2004).

text.text: For theory, the results suggest separating two things that agency cues might do: shape how people categorise a machine, as a tool or as an agent, and shape how they evaluate it.
Sundar (2020) treats machine agency as a central cue in human-AI interaction; the present findings suggest that such a cue can move categorisation without detectably moving evaluation.
Because agency cues may invite mind perception and switch off the machine heuristic at the same time, their net effect on trust may depend on which of the two a context makes salient.

Models of trust in AI that treat perceived agency as a direct antecedent of trustworthiness beliefs may need to specify the conditions under which agency matters, such as repeated interaction, visible performance or real stakes.
For practice, the findings caution providers against expecting agentic branding to build trust on its own.
Describing an advisor as an autonomous thinker did not detectably make it seem more competent, honest or caring.
Evidence that bears directly on trustworthiness, such as transparent track records for ability and verifiable alignment with the client's interests for benevolence, is more likely to matter.
Presenting AI advisors as capable co-pilots that leave users in control may be a better design default than presenting them as autonomous pilots, although this too needs testing.
Several limitations bound these conclusions.
First, the investment decision was hypothetical, and incentive-compatible designs with real payoffs are needed to test whether trust matters more when money is at stake.
Second, the manipulation was a one-off framing delivered on two screens.
Agency perceptions and trust develop over repeated interaction, and an advisor that visibly acts on its own may affect trust differently from one that is merely described as autonomous.

Third, the manipulation had a moderate effect on perceived agency, and the two analysis screens differed in more than agency: the high-agency screen's "internal thoughts" also mentioned the options' volatility and past drawdowns, whereas the low-agency screen listed procedural steps only.
This extra risk information could have affected trust or allocations independently of agency.
Stronger manipulations that hold information constant would give agency a fairer test.
Fourth, the study was powered to detect medium effects; detecting small effects of d = 0.20 would require roughly 790 participants.
Finally, the sample consisted of UK adults on an online panel, and responses to agentic AI may differ across cultures and levels of financial literacy.

Future research could test whether an AI advisor can earn benevolence through consistent, well-aligned advice over time, and whether doing so unlocks the competence credit that agency framing alone did not.
It could also measure perceived unpredictability and betrayal risk directly, to test whether they offset the competence signal of agency in high-stakes domains.
As AI advisors become more capable, providers will be tempted to present them as autonomous agents.
This study suggests that the label does less than they might hope.

Framing an AI financial advisor as agentic changed what people believed the system was, but did not detectably change whether they thought it was good at the job, honest or on their side, and trust was not clearly linked to what they were willing to risk.
For designers and researchers alike, trust in AI appears to depend less on how agentic a machine seems than on evidence about what it can do and whose interests it serves.
